blocks.text: [II, 489] is. For by what chance I do not know, in Avicenna and others it is much more often written الورك [al-wark] alvvarco, although the true spelling is الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo. This is taught by all the Arabic lexicographers, and the barbarous name guaril is derived from it. Not to mention the critical observation found in Damir, in the chapter ورل [waral] Guaril: لا تلتقي الراء مع اللام الا في اربع مواضع الورل وهو الحيوان المذكور وارل اسم جبل والغرلة وهو القلفة وحرل وهو ضرب من الحجارة [lā taltaqī al-rāʾ maʿa al-lām illā fī arbaʿ mawāḍiʿ al-waral wa-huwa al-ḥayawān al-madhkūr wa-Waral ism jabal wa-al-ghurla wa-hiya al-qulfa wa-ḥaral wa-huwa ḍarb min al-ḥijāra]. Re does not occur together with Lam (that is, R with L) except in four places. 1. In alvvarlo, the name of the animal discussed above. 2. In Aral, the name of a mountain, discussed above. 3. In alghorla, which means foreskin (like the Hebrew ערלה). 4. In charal, which is a kind of stone. These, then, are the four ancient versions, the Syriac, the Samaritan and the two Arabic, for which the anaka is a species of lizard. I have weighty reasons for adding my vote to theirs. 1. Because צב tsab, that is, the land crocodile, had preceded, and four other species of lizards are immediately added [col. 1066], as will be clear from what follows. Hence the anaka seems to belong to the same genus. For the mygale, or any other animal, would have been inserted in a less fitting place among so many species of lizards. 2. From the Hebrew אנקה anaka the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, has plainly arisen. For these two words (apart from the ending, which is Hebrew in the one and Syriac in the other) differ in no respect, except that the Syrians changed the Hebrew NUN into MEM, and nothing is more frequent in those languages than this change. Thus among the Chaldeans or Syrians "strong" is ܚܣܝܢ chasin and ܚܣܝܡ chasim; "reason" ܛܥܢܐ taana and ܛܥܡܐ taama; "nymph" ܢܝܢܦܐ ninphe and ܢܝܡܦܐ nimphe; "club" ܩܘܪܢܣܐ kurnesa and ܩܘܪܡܙܐ kurmeza; the terebinth, or the tree that bears the pistachio, ܒܘܛܡܐ butem, as in Hebrew בוטן boten. And in Arabic "thumb" is ابهام [ibhām] ibham for the Hebrew בהן bohen; as "to grow fat" is دسم [dasama] dasama for the Hebrew דשן dasen; and "to sing" is رنم [ranima] ranima for the Hebrew רנן ranan. In Ethiopic ዘመወ፡ zamavva, he committed fornication, for the Hebrew ונה zana; እድሜ፡ edem, time, for the Chaldee עדן iddan; አደመ፡ adam, pleasant, sweet, from the Hebrew עדן adan, to delight oneself. Such is the Egyptian ΜΕΤΩΠΟΝ, a kind of ointment, from the Hebrew נטף nataph or the Chaldee נטופא netopha; ΜΕΙΣΙ, serpent, from the Hebrew נחש naas. So too the Egyptian city of Memphis is called by the Prophets now נוף Noph, now מוף Moph. By the same pattern the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha here is derived from the Hebrew אנקה anaka, with N and M interchanged. Therefore, whatever the Syriac amaktha may be, it is highly probable that the Hebrew anaka is the very same. Now it is certain that ܐܡܩܬܐ is a kind of lizard, namely the stellio, Prov. XXX, 28, where it stands in the Syriac [II, 490] Paraphrase for the Hebrew שממית semamith. Likewise in the Chaldee, by a μετάθεσιν [metathesin] of letters, אקמתא akmetha, which is the same thing. Therefore, just as the Syriac ܐܡܩܬܐ amaktha, or amkatha, and the Chaldee אקמתא akmetha is the stellio, so also is the Hebrew אנקה anaka. Hence it is that the Samaritan too renders אנקה anaka by * [?] semamitha, that is, stellio; and both Arabic versions by الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, or الورك [al-wark] alvvarco, a kind of lizard close to the stellio, which many therefore take for the stellio, because it is similar in form. Accordingly Alkazuinius says of it: هو العظيم من شكل الوزغ وسوام ابرص [huwa al-ʿaẓīm min shakl al-wazagh wa-sawām abraṣ] This is large, of the same form as the guezga and the savvamabras, that is, as the smaller and larger stellios. This is taken from Avicenna. And Alcamus: الورل دابة كالضب والعظيم من اشكال الوزغ [al-waral dābba ka-al-ḍabb wa-al-ʿaẓīm min ashkāl al-wazagh] Alvvarlo (commonly guaril), an animal like the dhab (or land crocodile). And it is large among those which have the form of the guezga, or stellio. 3. In Hebrew אנקה anaka means a groan and a shrill cry, such as is uttered in great mourning. Should anyone deny that the stellio can be so named, as if it were a mute animal, he will be refuted by these words of Pliny on the stellio of Greece, book 29, chapter 4: This the Greeks call colotes, and ascalabotes, and galeotes. It does not occur in Italy. For it is full of freckles, has a harsh shrill cry, and * feeds. All of which are foreign to our stellios. Note has a harsh shrill cry. In Greek you would say τρισμοῦ τραχέος [trismou tracheos], whence it is rightly called אנקה anaka. And just as among the Hebrews a masculine plural is often formed from a feminine singular, as [col. 1067] יעלים from יעלה, and יענים from יענה, so from אנקה anaka the plural could be אנקים. And in the second Targum of Esther, chapter 1, verse 2, where, among the various animals that each utter their own cry before Solomon, אנקין בכיין anakin weeping, or wailing, are described, this should perhaps be understood not (as it is commonly taken) of the screaming of eagles, but of the cry and harsh shrill noise of stellios, which the very word אנקה anaka attests comes close to wailing. And for this very reason the Arabs, knowing at least this much, that the anaka was a kind of lizard, rendered it الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo, which itself also has a voice, though perhaps less sonorous. Hence Alcamus: ضغث الورل صوت [ḍaghatha al-waral ṣawwata] Dhagathsa alvvarlo, that is, it cried out. Those of our scholars who have published Arabic lexicons did not understand this sufficiently. For one rendered it The thigh gave a crack, another The hip sounded, because they read الورك [al-wark] alvvarco, which means ירך, i.e. hip. But they should have remembered that this very الورك [al-wark] occurs everywhere for الورل [al-waral], as we noted above ^{d)}. Not to mention that in the copy of τοῦ [tou] Alcamus which I used, الورل [al-waral] alvvarlo is quite correctly written. Therefore, what has hitherto escaped our scholars, let this stand as [II, 491] established: in the genus of lizards some are vocal, and among them is the stellio, which shrieks most shrilly. But we shall say more about the stellio in explaining the word שממית semamith.
